extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of 17th-century French letters / general readers of Mme de Sévigné
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and describing the qualities of witty epigrams and conversational wit as presented in 17th-century French letters (Madame de Coulanges / Madame de Sévigné material). Focuses on what makes remarks 'wit' and how they function socially and textually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit defined as graceful, easy, unexpected remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: « l'esprit de madame de Coulanges est une dignité. Cet esprit consistoit à dire avec grâce, avec aisance, des choses fines et imprévues, des mots vifs et piquans. »
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit should be delivered with grace and ease; it consists in fine, unforeseen (surprising) remarks and vivid, piquant words. The passage treats this as a positive, dignified quality—aim for naturalness, surprising turns, and vivid phrasing in witty remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigrams are delicate, fugitive, and context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: « Il semble qu'ils avoient quelque chose de plus délié, de plus fugitif, qui tenoit davantage aux circonstances des personnes, des lieux et du temps; ... ils perdroient beaucoup à être déplacés. »
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epigrams often rely on particular persons, places, moments, manner and tone; when removed from their original context they lose much of their force. Editorially or analytically, avoid transplanting context-dependent epigrams without noting the situational framing that gives them effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational wit: lively and brilliant turns
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation valued when it is « remplie de traits vifs et brillans. »
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social settings, successful wit manifests as lively, bright remarks—brief, striking turns of phrase that enliven conversation. Aim for vivacity and brilliance rather than long discursiveness when producing conversational humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as social capital / dignified trait
rubrics_metrics.description: The text treats esprit/wit as conferring social consideration: 'l'esprit de madame de Coulanges est une dignité', and anecdotes (e.g., 'Chaque péché de cette dame est une épigramme') present wit as a valued personal attribute even in moralizing comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit functions as a form of social capital: a person known for epigrams gains reputation and standing. When cultivating or judging humor in this period/context, consider social effects (status, reputation) alongside purely aesthetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial restraint: do not publish context-tied bon mots unannotated
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor explicitly refuses to transcribe any of Madame de Coulanges' epigrams into the Notice, saying they 'perdroient beaucoup à être déplacés' and therefore decides 'nous pensons qu'ils perdroient beaucoup à être déplacés; et ce motif nous détermine à n'en transporter aucun dans cette Notice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When compiling biography or criticism, exercise restraint and avoid reproducing context-bound witticisms without sufficient apparatus (context, speaker, occasion), since their effect depends on immediacy and circumstantial detail.
